meta.description: Not Plato. The line traces to Scottish minister John Watson (Ian Maclaren), 1897 — who actually wrote “Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Be kind, for everyone you meet is fighting a hard battle'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Plato. It traces to John Watson (Ian Maclaren), 1897, whose original word was “pitiful,” not “kind.”

answer.label: Not Plato — a paraphrase of Ian Maclaren (John Watson)
answer.sourceLine: The Plato credit is an anachronism of roughly 2,500 years. The saying traces to the Scottish minister and novelist John Watson, writing as Ian Maclaren, whose earliest documented version (British Weekly, Christmas 1897) read “Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle.” The now-familiar “Be kind … everyone you meet” wording is a later, softened paraphrase — not Plato’s words and not Watson’s exact ones.

source.excerpt: Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle.
trail: The Quote Investigator traces the earliest instance to Ian Maclaren (John Watson) in the British Weekly at Christmas 1897: “Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle.”
Wikipedia confirms Watson (1850–1907), a Free Church of Scotland minister who wrote as Ian Maclaren, as the source and notes the common misattributions to Plato and Philo of Alexandria.
Quote Investigator cites lexicographer Fred Shapiro observing that a Plato attribution is anachronistic by almost 2,500 years, since the saying is late-19th-century in origin.
source.excerptNote: Watson’s 1897 original. “Pitiful” here carries its now-archaic sense of ‘full of pity, compassionate.’ Over the 20th century it drifted to the gentler “Be kind, for everyone you meet is fighting a hard battle.”
source.rightsNote: Watson’s original line appeared in The British Weekly at Christmas 1897 — well before 1931 — so that text is in the public domain in the United States. The modern “Be kind” wording is an anonymous later paraphrase of that public-domain original, with no separately identifiable, in-copyright author.

author.name: John Watson (“Ian Maclaren”)
author.heading: Who was Ian Maclaren?
author.metaLine: 1850–1907 · Scottish Free Church minister & novelist (pen name Ian Maclaren)
author.bio: John Watson (1850–1907) was a Free Church of Scotland minister who won fame as a novelist under the pen name Ian Maclaren. His sentimental tales of rural Scottish life, above all Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush (1894), sold hundreds of thousands of copies and made him a leading figure of the “Kailyard” school. The compassionate aphorism now pinned on Plato began as a line of his pastoral counsel.

misattribution.heading: The tangled credit
misattribution.intro: This feel-good line is one of the internet’s most reliably misattributed quotes. It is pinned on ancient philosophers it long predates, while its actual author — and his actual words — are almost always dropped.

items.why: Countless quote sites credit Plato, but the saying is late-19th-century. As Quote Investigator notes (citing Fred Shapiro), a Plato attribution is off by almost 2,500 years.
A second popular but unsupported credit; no primary source in Philo’s works contains it, and it, too, would predate the documented origin by many centuries.
Even crediting Watson, the popular “Be kind … everyone you meet” form is a later softening of his original “Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle,” per the QI chronology.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented version is John Watson’s (Ian Maclaren’s) 1897 line “Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle” — not Plato, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Watson delivered the thought as pastoral counsel, and its power lay in the old sense of pitiful — not ‘pathetic,’ but ‘full of pity.’ As that sense faded, editors and reciters swapped in “kind,” and “every man” broadened to “everyone you meet.”
The migration onto Plato is a textbook case of authority-borrowing: a modern maxim gains gravitas when draped over an ancient name, and repetition on quote sites hardens the mistake.
context.pull: “Be pitiful” became “Be kind” — and a Scottish minister became Plato.
